title: On the Existence of an Extremal Function for the Delsarte Extremal Problem

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph beginning "It may happen that the class G_G(Ω) is empty"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The argument reads: "if f is positive definite, then |f(g)| ≤ f(0) for all g ∈ G, and if 0 ∉ int Ω, then f(0) = 0, and hence f is identically 0." The inference "0 ∉ int Ω ⟹ f(0) = 0" is a non sequitur as written: the bound |f(g)| ≤ f(0) says nothing about the value of f(0). The correct argument needs continuity: if f(0) > 0 then {f > 0} is an open neighbourhood of 0 contained in supp f_+ ⊂ Ω, forcing 0 ∈ int Ω. The conclusion is true but the stated justification does not establish it.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2 (Notation and preliminaries), definition of P(G) and P_1(G) vs. Introduction
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Introduction defines "P_1(G) is the collection of continuous positive definite functions f : G → ℝ satisfying f(0) = 1" (real-valued), whereas Section 2 defines P(G) ⊂ C(G) as the continuous positive definite functions with C(G) the space of continuous complex-valued functions, and then P_1(G) := {f ∈ P(G) : f(0)=1} with no real-valuedness restriction. Since the whole construction uses the positive part f_+ (meaningful only for real-valued f), the two definitions of the same symbol are inconsistent.

"By outer regularity of the Haar measure on G, there is an open identity neighbourhood U in G containing Ω with λ_G(U) < ∞." Outer regularity only yields an open set U ⊇ Ω of finite measure; it gives no reason for U to be a neighbourhood of the identity (Ω need not even contain 0 in the generality assumed in Theorem 3, where Ω is merely a measurable set of finite measure). The extra property is in fact never used in the remainder of the proof, so the claim is both unjustified and spurious.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 8, sentence "Since G_G(Ω) is contained in a closed, bounded, and hence a weakly sequentially compact subset of L^2(G)"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Closedness plus boundedness does not imply weak sequential compactness in a Hilbert space (e.g. an orthonormal set is closed and bounded but its weak limit 0 is not in the set); convexity (or weak closedness) is required. What is actually needed and true is simply that bounded sequences in the reflexive space L^2(G) have weakly convergent subsequences. Moreover the boundedness of G_G(Ω) in L^2 (which follows from ||f||_2^2 ≤ ||f||_∞||f||_1 ≤ 2λ_G(Ω)) is asserted without proof.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3, case 0 ∉ int Ω
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "Then, both G_G(Ω) and G_H(Ω) are empty. Therefore, both sides of (1) are equal to 0." The Delsarte constant is defined as a supremum; the supremum over the empty set is conventionally −∞ (or undefined), not 0. No convention for sup ∅ is stated anywhere in the paper, so the asserted value 0 is unjustified.

"As in Theorem 8, (f_n)_{n∈ℕ} converges to f uniformly on the compact subsets of H, and hence (f̃_n) converges to f̃ ..." — no sequence (f_n) has been introduced in this proof; only the extremal function f ∈ G_H(Ω) obtained from Theorem 8 is defined. The approximating extremal sequence on H and the verification that its trivial extensions form a D_G(Ω)-extremal sequence are never specified.

predicted_errors.error_location: End of Introduction, claim that integrability is automatic
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "However, in this case it follows from f ∈ P_1(G) together with λ_G(Ω) < ∞." Only ∫ f_+ ≤ λ_G(Ω) is immediate; the integrability of f_- for a continuous positive definite function that is not a priori in L^1 is a nontrivial fact (it requires an approximate-identity/Bochner argument). The assertion is made with neither proof nor citation, even though the paper elsewhere relies on integrability (e.g. to justify ∫(f_n)_- ≤ ∫(f_n)_+ in (6)).
